proposals.relationship: Thierno Diop identifies Marx’s historical-materialist method as an intellectual resource in Cheikh Anta Diop’s study of African civilizations, despite Diop’s refusal of dogmatic application and disagreement with particular theses.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation, not a self-declared Marxist identity or inferred party membership. Thierno1998:87 quotes Diop’s1954preface from1979:18–19 about his inspiration and African application;110 explicitly concludes Marxist methodological influence. Bianchini2023:86/nn14–15 corroborates selective use. No original Diop preface or Marx work was read here, and support for the method does not endorse all Diop conclusions.

proposals.relationship: As Bianchini documents, Diop faults Capital for leaving unclear how capitalism operates outside Europe when it is introduced through European expansion rather than arising from local historical development.
proposals.evidence_note: Bounded explicit criticism mediated through Bianchini2023:86/n16 quoting Diop,L’Afrique noire précoloniale(1960),112. This is an objection about scope and application, not a rejection of Marx’s entire method or proof that Capital lacks every relevant discussion. Original1960book and Capital remain unread. Thierno’s separate108/n10 causal-order objection to a CapitalIIIpassage has an ambiguous Diop1973:260reference and is retained as a held additional argument rather than silently merged into this specific claim.

proposals.relationship: Okpewho identifies Nietzsche’s Birth of Tragedy as a particular resource for Diop’s contrast between Greek tragic guilt and the optimistic Egyptian and African cultural model in Cultural Unity.
proposals.evidence_note: Named substantive scholarly mediation: Okpewho1981:596 explicitly states Diop relies on Nietzsche’s essay for the165–180discussion, continued597;600 compares Soyinka’s different reading of the same resource. This asserts a resource relationship, not agreement with Nietzsche as a whole, nor validation of Diop’s racial/cultural dichotomy, which Okpewho criticizes. Diop’s1962edition and Nietzsche original are unread here; no personal contact or reciprocal influence is asserted.
